text: Half the people who reviewed this free demo had already played it for eleven hours. Not one of them quit inside ten minutes. Not one.
And the people leaving negative reviews had played longer than the people leaving positive ones.
Guildrun is a PvE autobattler roguelike. You build a team, you bend heroes out of their class, and you watch the fight resolve itself.
Nearly two thousand reviews, ninety percent positive, and about two and a half thousand people in it as I record this. That's the biggest demo I've taken apart.
It's also the first one where the file list told me the team had done this before.
Start with the awkward part. This is an I L two C P P build, so all the C sharp is fused into one Game Assembly file.
In the last teardown that was a dead end. There's no folder of package names to read.
Except it isn't quite a dead end. Any assembly that shipped with embedded resources leaves its name behind in a data file, and Steam lists those.
Twenty four names came out. Here's what a team that has shipped before installs.
Sentry, with six assemblies and a native crash handler behind it. They've shipped a patch every single week since January. That's what makes that survivable.
S Q Lite, because the demo alone has three hundred relics and a hundred items. At some point that stops being a pile of JSON files.
N Log for structured logging. R three and System Reactive for event streams. Threading Channels for the producer-consumer work.
And Z Link, which exists for one reason: doing LINQ without allocating. You install that when you've been bitten by garbage collection hitches.
None of that is exciting. It's the stuff you only know to install because something went wrong on the last project.
Compare the solo demo I took apart two episodes ago. Its entire third party list was one entry: Discord rich presence.
Neither is wrong. But if you're about to start your second project, that list up there is a shopping list.
Audio is F MOD with Resonance, same as the last one. Networking is nanosockets, a thin U D P layer.
Then the number I stared at for a while.
The demo is ten and a half gigabytes on disk. The download is one point one seven.
That's an eighty nine percent saving. Which means the files sitting on your drive are barely compressed at all.
My first thought was that somebody forgot the import settings. My second thought was to read the store page.
Minimum requirements: fifteen gigabytes of storage, and a line that says H D D okay, no S S D required.
Uncompressed assets cost disk and save C P U. On a hard drive with no decompression to do, they load faster. My read is that this is deliberate.
They spent ten gigabytes of somebody's drive to keep the game playable on old hardware. Tell me in the comments if I've got that backwards.
There are also twenty two scenes in here. The last two games I took apart shipped one each and built everything at runtime. This one is authored in the editor.
So the engineering is careful. The fight in the reviews is about something else entirely.
Performance barely comes up. Ten mentions positive, two negative. Nobody is complaining about the build.
They're complaining about balance. Certain combinations only, dead heroes, and a random draw that decides your run before you play it.
And that's why the negative reviewers had fifteen hours in. You don't find a balance ceiling in an hour. You find it after you've mastered the thing.
Which is a very different problem from the demos where people quit in the first hour.
Here's the whole teardown on one card.
Unity, I L two C P P, C sharp. A stack full of things you only reach for the second time around. Ten gigabytes of deliberately uncompressed art.
Worth a dip, and be careful, because eleven hours is the median.
If you're starting your next project, take the boring half of that list. Crash reporting on day one is the cheapest thing you will ever install.
That's my read from the outside. If you made this and I got something wrong, say so and I'll pin the correction. Next time, another demo, another file list. This is Demo Dip.
